newsitem.title: CANADA: Free trade helped Canada's trade flows, study says.
newsitem.headline: Free trade helped Canada's trade flows, study says.

text.p: The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) have had a significant positive impact on trade flows among Canada, the United States and Mexico, an independent Canadian research organization said on Wednesday.

The study conducted by the conservative C.D. Howe Institute concludes that Canada's investment performance was strong from 1989, when the trade deal with the United States came into effect, until 1995, the last year in the study.
Free trade has not done much for jobs or pay in Canada, however.

"While the agreements are not to blame for Canada's disappointing labor market performance during the period, there is also little direct evidence that they helped to spur employment and wages," the institute said in a statement.
The free trade deals have spurred growth in liberalized sectors, with those sectors outpacing growth in other sectors or with other countries, the study said.
Surprisingly, North America as a whole did not become any more attractive as a destination for foreign direct investment from 1989 to 1995, the study said.

As for manufacturing, the study argues that the best and worst performers in the sector are found in industries least directly affected by free trade. Sectors that are the most sensitive to free trade saw no change in their share of employment, but their wages fell somewhat.

"While the FTA and NAFTA have not had the negative effect on employment that some had feared, they are far from having been a cure for Canada's poor competitiveness and employment performance," said Daniel Schwanen, the study's author.
"Factors other than North American free trade must account for Canada's problem of hesitant growth in employment, productivity and earnings."
